findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of match_count in should_block?
findings.body: The `should_block?` method reads `match_count`, increments it in Ruby memory, then calls `save`. Under concurrent requests (e.g., two signups with the same blocked email simultaneously), both requests can read the same value, increment it, and save, resulting in a lost update. Use an atomic SQL update like `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` instead.

findings.title: save can fail silently in should_block?, losing match statistics
findings.body: `record.save` returns false on failure (e.g., validation error) without raising. If the save fails, the match_count increment and last_match_at update are silently lost. Since this is called during user validation, a failure here would go unnoticed. Consider using `update_columns` to bypass validations/callbacks, or at minimum `save!` with error handling.

findings.title: Validator has write side-effect: should_block? mutates database during validation
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a database write (incrementing match_count, updating last_match_at) every time it is called. Since this is invoked from a model validator, any call to `user.valid?` — including dry-run checks, admin previews, or repeated validations before save — will increment the counter. This makes match_count unreliable as a metric and introduces unexpected writes in contexts that should be read-only. The counting logic should be separated from the blocking check, or moved to an after_save/after_create callback.

findings.title: Email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing blocked emails to be bypassed
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` performs a case-sensitive comparison. If an admin blocks `spammer@evil.com` but a user signs up with `Spammer@Evil.com`, the lookup will not find the record and the email will not be blocked. The codebase has an `Email.downcase` helper used elsewhere (e.g., `users_controller.rb#change_email`). The email should be normalized (downcased) before lookup, and ideally also normalized before storage via a `before_validation` callback.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex does not escape all special characters
findings.body: `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` only escapes dots, but the setting value could contain other regex metacharacters (e.g., `+` in `sub+domain.com`). This could cause incorrect matching or regex errors. Use `Regexp.escape` on each domain segment, or split on the delimiter and escape individually.

findings.title: rejectedEmails persists across modal sessions on singleton controller
findings.body: `rejectedEmails` is initialized as `Em.A([])` on the controller prototype. In Ember, controllers are singletons, so this array accumulates rejected emails across multiple opens of the create-account modal. If an admin later unblocks an email, the client will still reject it until a full page reload. The array should be cleared when the modal is opened or the controller is reset.

findings.title: No test coverage for whitelist/blacklist logic in EmailValidator
findings.body: The spec only tests the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` path (stubbed). The whitelist and blacklist logic that was moved from `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator` has no test coverage in this new spec file. If the refactor introduced a regression in domain matching, it would not be caught.
